Subject: Post-call recap: performance SLOs & context window follow-up

Hi Alice / FinCo team,

Thanks again for the call earlier — really useful to surface the latency and context-window constraints for your use cases. Quick recap and a few follow-ups so we can scope a benchmark: 

1) Goals & SLOs you mentioned
- 95th pct latency target: <= 250ms for UI token streaming responsiveness where possible (hard SLO for critical flows).
- Throughput: steady-state of ~5-10 qps, peak ~15 qps during high-traffic events.
- Concurrency: 10-20 concurrent users making interactive requests.
- Streaming: progressive token streaming is required for the customer-facing chat UX.

2) Context / token needs
- You indicated long-document reference is important; rough estimate was max context window around 60k tokens (this includes both input and any expected output generation). Typical request today: ~10k input tokens and up to 5k output tokens for synthesis tasks, but there are occasional batch jobs with much larger inputs.

3) Key questions for our tech team to size benchmarks and recommend model variants:
- Can you share a sample set of representative prompts (anonymized) and average token counts?
- Which flows require strict 95p latency vs. which can be best-effort / async?
- Are fallbacks acceptable (shorter context + retrieval) if we can't meet the hard SLO at the largest context sizes?

Attached: finco_slo_matrix.xlsx (blank SLO template) — we'll fill this in with target numbers after we get sample prompts.

Next steps: we’ll run a focused benchmark once we have the prompts and confirm a week to demo results (aiming for the week of Dec 8).

Thanks — Marissa

Thanks Marissa — appreciate the recap. A few clarifications from our side: 

- Context window: we need the ability to reference up to ~65k tokens in the largest workflows (legal/contract ingestion). For interactive chat, the typical active context is closer to 10-20k tokens (input + short histories).
- Output sizes: usually 1-5k tokens for most summaries; some synthesis jobs generate up to 10k tokens.
- Concurrency/QPS: our expected steady-state is 8-12 qps across the product, peaks at ~15-18 qps during reporting. Concurrency per user is usually 1-2 simultaneous requests, but we expect batches from scheduled jobs.
- Streaming is required for the main UX; initial token should be near-instant for perceived responsiveness (customer expects the first token within 200-300ms if possible).

We can share an anonymized prompt set — attaching a small sample separately. Also, SOC2 and data retention details will come from our security team; we'll share contacts if you need more.

Goal: keep customer experience snappy for interactive flows and acceptable for background jobs. Let us know if lower-latency fallbacks are feasible and what tradeoffs you’d recommend.

—Alice

Subject: RE: Post-call recap: performance SLOs & context window follow-up

Hi Alice / team — technical follow-up and recommended approach. I pulled some representative numbers based on our 64k-capable model variants and typical infra configs. Key tradeoffs first, then numbers: 

High-level tradeoffs:
- Large context windows (40-65k tokens) increase memory pressure and KV-cache overhead on GPU; that reduces concurrency per GPU and increases tail latency.
- Streaming helps UX but has two components: initial generation latency (time to first token) and sustained per-token latency. Initial token tends to be higher because of model startup/IO and decoder priming.
- Batching improves throughput but increases per-request latency variance; continuous batching with short windows (10-30ms) is the usual compromise.

Recommended model + infra options:
- For interactive flows up to ~20k context, we recommend Redwood-Large-32k quantized for best latency/cost balance. That supports moderate concurrency (6-12 concurrent interactive sessions per GPU depending on token lengths).
- For workloads requiring 64k context, use Redwood-XL-64k (larger memory footprint, fewer concurrent sessions per GPU — expect ~1-3 concurrent interactive sessions per GPU for sustained 64k contexts). Consider hybrid approach: long-context for background/synthesis jobs, and retrieval/windowing for interactive sessions.

Empirical latency estimates (approx; 1 GPU serving with continuous batching and prefix cache where applicable):
- Context 8k (input 4k + output 1k): initial token ~110-150ms; steady per-token generation ~18-30ms; 95p token latency for short sessions ~<200ms.
- Context 20k (input 15k + output 2k): initial token ~150-220ms; per-token ~25-40ms; 95p token latency ~200-350ms depending on concurrency and batching window.
- Context 40-65k: initial token ~220-450ms; per-token ~30-60ms; tail latencies can spike >500ms at higher concurrency.

Notes on meeting your 95p <=250ms target for interactive streaming:
- For consistent <=250ms at 95p, we can meet that for most interactive flows if active context is kept <=~20k and concurrency is limited per GPU (or routed to lower-latency dedicated capacity).
- For >40k contexts, expect the 95p to breach 250ms unless we accept lower concurrency, heavier provisioning, or fallback strategies (retrieval + short context).

Optimizations we can apply during benchmarking:
- Prefix/KV caching for repeated system tokens and shared documents to reduce per-request work.
- Adaptive batching windows: smaller windows for interactive requests to prioritize latency.
- Quantized kernels and kernel fusion for larger sequences to reduce per-token time.
- Hybrid routing policy: interactive requests go to low-latency pool; large-batch synth jobs go to high-memory pool.

Attachments: redwood_latency_notes.pdf (contains detailed per-token microbenchmarks) and the finco_slo_matrix.xlsx Marissa referenced.

Next steps I recommend:
1) Receive anonymized prompt set + representative token histograms (Marissa/Alice)
2) Run two benchmark passes: interactive (sample of 10-20k contexts) and long-context (40-65k) with streaming turned on; record p50/p95/p99 token latencies and cost/Ops.
3) Validate fallbacks (retrieval + shorter context) on a small subset to quantify UX delta.

I can lead the benchmark and share a Jupyter notebook with the workload harness. If you can provide the sample prompts and a target date for the demo (Marissa suggested week of Dec 8), we’ll schedule infra and prioritize the interactive pass first.
